column1: In the previous trace, root.getSize()'s loop calls sub.getSize() — which is a completely separate invocation of the SAME method, just running on a different object (sub instead of root). What's the technical term for a method that calls itself (directly or, as here, through calling the same method on a different object of the same type) as part of solving a larger problem?,"Recursion — Folder.getSize() solving the ""total size of this folder"" problem by calling getSize() on its children, some of which may themselves be folders needing the exact same kind of solving",Overriding — since sub.getSize() overrides root.getSize(),Delegation — since sub is a completely unrelated class to root,Composition — since sub is composed inside root,,1,"This is precisely what recursion means: the same method being invoked again to solve the same kind of subproblem, just on a smaller/different piece of the structure.",1

Given the previous insight — that a container can optionally contribute its OWN value on top of its children's values — sketch what would need to change if Folder itself also had a fixed metadata overhead cost (say, every folder takes up 4096 bytes just to exist on disk, separate from its contents)?,This is impossible to represent since FileSystemItem only has one method,This would require abandoning the Composite structure entirely and switching to a completely different pattern,"Folder.getSize()'s total variable would need to start at 4096 instead of 0, then still loop over and sum up all children — same structural pattern as Manager, just with a folder-specific base value instead of a salary",File would need to be modified to account for folder overhead,,3,"Adding a container's own base contribution is a small, localized change to the container's own method — no structural change to the pattern is needed.",1

Manager.addDirectReport(Employee employee) accepts an Employee, not specifically an IndividualContributor. What real-world structure does this enable, mirroring what Folder.add(FileSystemItem item) enables for folders-within-folders?,"Employee must be a concrete class, not an interface, for this to compile","Manager objects can never be added as another Manager's direct report, only IndividualContributors can",This only works if Manager and IndividualContributor are declared in the same file,"A Manager can report to another Manager — since Manager implements Employee, a Manager object satisfies addDirectReport()'s parameter type just like an IndividualContributor does, letting org charts nest to any depth (VP, Director, Manager, IC)",,4,"Accepting the shared interface type is exactly what allows a Manager to report to another Manager, mirroring Folder-within-Folder nesting.",1

A UI framework has UIComponent interface with void render(). Button implements UIComponent just draws itself. Panel implements UIComponent holds a List<UIComponent> children and its render() loops over them calling child.render() on each, then draws its own border. Is this the same Composite shape as File/Folder, and what's Panel's equivalent of Folder's "own contribution" (like the folder metadata overhead discussed earlier)?,"Yes, same shape — Button is the leaf, Panel is the container
column2: Panel's ""own contribution"" is drawing its border, which happens in addition to (not instead of) rendering all its children, mirroring how Manager adds its own salary on top of its reports' totals","Yes, but Panel cannot contain another Panel, only Buttons","No — this requires the Decorator pattern instead, since Panel adds its own behavior (drawing a border)","No — UI components can never be structured as a Composite pattern since rendering is visual, not numeric",,1,"The pattern generalizes cleanly beyond numeric aggregation — Panel's border-drawing is its own contribution, analogous to Manager's salary or a hypothetical folder's metadata overhead.",1

column1: In the UI example, could a Panel contain another Panel as one of its children (a panel nested inside a panel, nested inside a panel, arbitrarily deep — like nested divs)?,"Yes, but only up to a hardcoded maximum depth of 3","Yes — since Panel implements UIComponent, and children is typed List<UIComponent>, a Panel satisfies its own container's type requirement, exactly the same mechanism that let Folders nest inside Folders",No — only one level of Panel nesting is possible in any Composite structure,No — Panel would need to extend Button first for this to work,,2,Arbitrary nesting depth is always available once the container implements the same interface it accepts as children — no artificial depth limit exists.,1

A menu system has MenuComponent interface with void print(). MenuItem implements MenuComponent prints its own name and price. Menu implements MenuComponent holds children and, when printed, prints its own name as a header, THEN loops through children calling print() on each. If a Menu named "Desserts" contains two MenuItems ("Cake", "IceCream") and a nested Menu named "Seasonal" containing one more MenuItem ("PumpkinPie"), trace the exact print order.,This cannot be determined without knowing the price of each item,"""Desserts"", ""Seasonal"", ""Cake"", ""IceCream"", ""PumpkinPie"" — headers always print before any items regardless of nesting","""Desserts"" header, then ""Cake"", then ""IceCream"", then ""Seasonal"" header, then ""PumpkinPie"" — the nested Menu's own print() call handles printing its own header before looping through its own children, and this entire nested call happens exactly when the outer loop reaches that child","""Cake"", ""IceCream"", ""PumpkinPie"", ""Desserts"", ""Seasonal"" — all items print first, headers print last",,3,"Tracing execution order in a tree structure means following exactly when each nested call happens relative to the loop that triggers it, not assuming a fixed global ordering.",1

A tester wants to verify that root.getSize() correctly sums nested folders WITHOUT needing to construct real File objects with real byte sizes. Given File implements FileSystemItem, what's a clean way to test Folder.getSize() in isolation?,You would need to modify Folder to add a special test-only method,Testing requires reflection to access the private children field directly,Folder.getSize() cannot be tested without real files existing on disk,"Create a lightweight test class implementing FileSystemItem whose getSize() just returns a fixed fake value (e.g. always 100), add a few instances of it to a Folder, and assert the folder's getSize() sums them correctly — no real File objects needed at all",,4,Coding to the interface rather than a concrete class is exactly what allows lightweight test doubles to stand in during testing — same benefit seen throughout the course.,1

Given the previous answer, what does this reveal about why Folder depends on FileSystemItem (the interface) rather than depending directly on File (the concrete class) in its children field and add() method?,"Depending on the interface rather than the concrete class is exactly what makes Folder usable with ANY object satisfying FileSystemItem — real files, other folders, or even test doubles — without Folder's own code ever needing to change to support a new kind of item",This only matters for testing purposes and has no other benefit,Folder depends on FileSystemItem only because Java requires all List fields to be typed to interfaces,There's no real reason
column2: depending on File directly would work identically,,1,Interface-based dependency is what makes Folder open to new item types (real or fake) without ever needing modification.,1

column1: Suppose someone adds a Shortcut class — a lightweight pointer to another FileSystemItem elsewhere in the tree, implementing FileSystemItem by just delegating getSize() to whatever it points to. Does adding Shortcut require ANY changes to Folder or File?,Yes — Folder.getSize() would need a new branch specifically checking for Shortcut objects,"No — since Shortcut implements FileSystemItem, it can be added to any Folder's children list and participate in getSize() calculations exactly like a File or nested Folder would, with zero changes to either existing class",Yes — FileSystemItem itself would need a new method added just for Shortcut,"No, but only if Shortcut is placed in the same package as Folder",,2,New implementers of the shared interface plug in with zero changes to existing container or leaf classes — the same OCP payoff seen throughout the course.,1

This is the same "closed for modification, open for extension" property seen with Factory Method and Observer earlier in the course. State precisely which existing classes stay completely untouched when a new FileSystemItem implementer (like Shortcut) is introduced, and which new classes get written.,"FileSystemItem needs a new abstract method added, forcing every existing implementer to be updated",Folder.getSize()'s loop needs a new conditional branch added for the new type,"FileSystemItem, File, and Folder all stay completely untouched — only one new class, Shortcut implements FileSystemItem, needs to be written, and it becomes usable everywhere FileSystemItem is expected immediately",File needs to be modified to recognize Shortcut objects,,3,"This is the cleanest possible extension case: one new class, zero edits to anything already written.",1

A teammate proposes an alternative design: instead of Folder implements FileSystemItem, make Folder a completely separate, unrelated class with its own getFolderSize() method (different name, different interface, no shared type with File). What capability is immediately lost with this alternative?,"This alternative would actually be more flexible, since it separates folders and files completely",File.getSize() would stop working entirely,"Nothing is lost — this alternative works identically, just with different method names","Folders could no longer contain other folders (since add(FileSystemItem item) would no longer accept a Folder, as Folder wouldn't satisfy that type anymore), and any code wanting to compute a size would need to check ""is this a File or a Folder?"" and call the correct differently-named method manually — reintroducing exactly the type-checking Composite exists to eliminate",,4,Breaking the shared-interface requirement immediately reintroduces the type-checking problem Composite is specifically designed to eliminate.,1

Tie together everything traced across File/Folder, IndividualContributor/Manager, Button/Panel, and MenuItem/Menu. In one sentence, what's the exact structural requirement that must hold for a "leaf and container" pair to actually work as Composite, and what capability breaks the moment that requirement is violated?,"The container must implement the exact same interface as the leaf (not merely hold leaves as children) — the moment the container implements a different interface, or the leaf-accepting method is narrowed to reject the container type, nesting one container inside another becomes impossible, and calling code is forced back into explicit type-checking to distinguish leaves from containers","The container must always start its aggregation value at zero, or the pattern is considered invalid","The leaf must always be declared before the container in the source file, or the pattern won't compile correctly","There is no structural requirement — any two classes can be arbitrarily called ""leaf"" and ""container"" regardless of their interfaces",,1,This is the single load-bearing rule underlying every example traced in this quiz — shared interface between leaf and container is what makes arbitrary-depth nesting and uniform treatment possible at all.,2
